package.name: Allocator
package.description: Allocation contracts and the allocators that meet them

modules.name: Arena
modules.header:
An allocator that hands out storage by advancing a pointer, and takes it all back at once.
An arena is the right shape whenever a program builds a lot of small things whose lives all end together: a parse
tree, one request's working set, a frame's worth of geometry. Allocation is an addition and a bounds check, and
nothing is tracked per allocation, because nothing is released per allocation.
Storage comes from a backing allocator in blocks. When a block cannot serve a request the arena takes another,
twice the size of the last, so a long-lived arena stops going back to the system rather than asking once per
allocation. A request larger than a whole block gets a block of its own.
`Reset` is what makes an arena worth reusing: it rewinds every allocation while keeping the largest block, so the
next round of work runs without asking the system for anything at all.
The arena prohibits copying and `~Arena` releases its blocks. `Handle` is a storable interface adapter over the
same owner; because it contains a raw pointer, it must not outlive or survive a move of the arena.

modules.name: Box
modules.header:
One value, on the heap, with exactly one owner.
A `Box<T>` is the smallest thing that owns an allocation: it holds a value of `T` and the allocator that gave it
the storage, and it destroys the value and releases the storage when it goes. Copying is prohibited, so handing
one to a function or another binding requires an explicit move.
The allocator is held as an interface value rather than a type parameter, so `Box<T>` has one parameter rather
than two and a container of boxes does not have to name which allocator each came from. The cost is one indirect
call per allocation and release, which against the cost of allocating is not a cost at all.
Construction takes the value by value, which means it is consumed. If the allocation fails the value is destroyed
rather than leaked, and nothing half-built exists — there is no state in which a `Box` holds an allocation it
cannot release.
A box is *returned* rather than written through an out-parameter. Ownership is what forces it: the compiler
tracks a binding's initialization, and a write through a pointer is invisible to that tracking, so a box delivered
that way would be owned by a binding the compiler believes owns nothing. Returning it makes the transfer visible,
and a failure comes back through the same return: `Create` returns `Box<T> ! AllocError`.

modules.name: Contract
modules.header:
What every allocator in this package promises, written as a bound a generic can require.
The contract is deliberately small: take a layout and give back storage, take it back, and grow or shrink a block
in place where that is possible. Everything else — pooling, arenas, tracking — is an implementation of these
three, not an addition to them.
Four promises hold for every implementation, and a caller may rely on them without knowing which allocator it has:
  - **The address satisfies the layout.** A block handed back is aligned to what was asked for, always.
  - **The contents are undefined.** Nothing here zeroes. A caller wanting zeroed storage clears it, or asks the
    page layer, which does zero because the operating system does.
  - **A release must match its allocation.** The same pointer, and a layout equal to the one it was given with.
    An allocator may check that or may not; passing a different layout is undefined either way, because the
    allocator needs the size to know what it is taking back.
  - **A failure leaves everything alone.** A failed allocation gives no storage and takes none; a failed
    reallocation leaves the original block exactly as it was, valid and still the caller's to release.
A zero-sized layout is legal. Every allocator here answers it with a non-null, correctly aligned address that
nothing may be read from or written to, and which must still be released. That is cheaper than a null case every
caller has to branch on, and it keeps a zero-length collection from being a special shape.
A *reallocation* down to a zero-sized layout is one of those, and reports the same address a zero-sized allocation
would. Two of the allocators here used to hand back the block they were rewinding off of instead, which left the
caller holding an address that `Deallocate` then refused — a zero-sized release must arrive with the empty block.

modules.name: Error
modules.header:
Why an allocation did not happen.
An allocator that fails has to say so in a way the caller can act on, and "null" is not that: it cannot tell a
request that was too large from one the system refused from one the allocator was never able to serve. These are
the four answers, and every allocator in this package gives one of them.
Every case is a failure. An allocator returns its address or completion through a native fallible, `T ! AllocError`,
so success is the other channel rather than a member of this enum, and a result nobody handles is diagnosed.

modules.name: FixedBuffer
modules.header:
An allocator that hands out storage from a buffer the caller already has, and never asks anyone for more.
This is the arena's shape without the arena's appetite: allocation is an addition and a bounds check, everything
is reclaimed at once, and when the buffer runs out the answer is `OutOfMemory` rather than another block. That
makes it the allocator for the places where allocation must not happen — a fixed working set, a signal-safe path,
an embedded target with no allocator underneath at all.
It owns nothing, so it has no destructor and the buffer's life is entirely the caller's business. What it does
have is mutable state, and an allocator that is copied while it is being used would hand out the same storage
twice — so `Handle` is what implements `Allocator`, exactly as it is for the arena.

modules.name: Layout
modules.header:
What an allocation is asked for: a size in bytes and an alignment the address must be a multiple of.
A `Layout` exists so that the pair travels together and is checked once. Passing a size and an alignment as two
loose arguments is how an allocator ends up asked for an alignment that is not a power of two, or a size whose
rounding overflows — neither of which most allocators check, and both of which produce an allocation that is
smaller or less aligned than the caller believes.
A `Layout` that exists is valid. `New` is the only way to build one and refuses what it cannot represent, so
nothing downstream has to check again.
`ForValue<T>` and `ForArray<T>` describe storage without constructing a value and use the type's actual alignment.

modules.name: Pool
modules.header:
An allocator that serves small blocks from free lists, one per size class, and reuses what is given back.
The arena is fast because it never reclaims. This is the allocator for the other shape: many small values whose
lives end at different times and in no particular order — list nodes, hash table entries, small strings. Both
allocation and release are a handful of instructions and a pointer swap, with no search and no coalescing.
A request is rounded up to one of a few power-of-two classes, and each class keeps its own list of blocks that
have been handed back. When a class runs dry the pool takes one chunk from a backing allocator and carves it into
blocks of that class, so the backing allocator sees one request per chunk rather than one per block.
Rounding up is what pays for the speed. A 17-byte request occupies a 32-byte block, and the 15 bytes are not
recoverable until the whole chunk is released — which is the trade a pool makes, and the reason it is not the
allocator to reach for when sizes vary widely.
A request too large for the largest class, or needing an alignment stricter than a chunk is taken at, is passed
straight to the backing allocator. That decision is made from the layout alone, so a release reaches the same
conclusion as the allocation it matches without the pool recording anything per block.
The pool prohibits copying and `~Pool` releases its chunks. `Handle` is a storable interface adapter over the
same owner; because it contains a raw pointer, it must not outlive or survive a move of the pool.

modules.name: System
modules.header:
The allocator that asks the operating system, and is the one everything else falls back to.
It is built on `Rux/Memory`'s page layer rather than on a C heap, which is what lets it honour an alignment
stricter than a machine word: pages come aligned to a page, and a header placed before the returned address
records what has to be given back.
The header is why a release needs its layout. The block handed to the caller is not the block taken from the
system — there is a header before it and padding before that — and the header holds the length to release. Both
the layout and the header are checked against each other, so a mismatched release is reported rather than
corrupting the next allocation.
This is a page-granular allocator, so a small allocation costs a whole page. That is the right shape for the
backing store of an arena or a pool, and the wrong one for a program allocating many small values directly --
which is what the arena and pool allocators in this package exist for.

doc.summary: A copyable interface adapter pointing at this arena.
doc.markdown:
A copyable interface adapter pointing at this arena.
`self` stays the caller's. Allocations through the handle update this arena rather than copied state.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.
The handle borrows the arena and must not outlive it, nor survive the arena being moved. Nothing here tracks
that: a handle held past its arena's life points at released storage.

doc.summary: Rewinds every allocation, keeping the largest block for the next round of work.
doc.markdown:
Rewinds every allocation, keeping the largest block for the next round of work.
`self` is borrowed mutably. Every pointer the arena ever handed out becomes invalid, including any still held
by a caller — an arena reclaims in one operation, which is what makes it fast and what makes this the one
dangerous call on it.
The kept block is the current one, which is the largest, so a second round of the same work runs without
asking the system for anything. Runs in time proportional to the number of blocks.
Nothing may be read from or written to any earlier allocation afterwards.

doc.summary: How many payload bytes the arena has handed out, summed over every block it holds.
doc.markdown:
How many payload bytes the arena has handed out, summed over every block it holds.
`self` is borrowed. Alignment padding between allocations counts as used. The tail a block was left with when
a request did not fit in it and the arena moved on to a new block is not counted: nothing was handed out of
it, and nothing will be until a `Reset`. Runs in time proportional to the number of blocks and allocates
nothing.
doc.returns: how many payload bytes the arena's blocks have handed out

doc.markdown:
How many blocks the arena holds.

doc.returns: how many blocks the arena holds

doc.markdown:
Gives every block back to the backing allocator.

doc.markdown:

doc.markdown:
Takes storage matching `layout` by advancing the arena's pointer.
`result` receives the address when this reports `None`. A zero-sized layout gives the shared empty block and
consumes none of the arena.
Takes a new block when the current one cannot serve the request, which is the only path here that can fail.
The storage lives until the arena is reset or destroyed, whichever comes first, and not one moment longer.

doc.summary: Accepts a release and reclaims only what it can.
doc.markdown:
Accepts a release and reclaims only what it can.
An arena reclaims in one operation, so an ordinary release has nothing to give back and reports `None` having
done nothing. The exception is the most recent allocation, whose space is rewound — which is what lets a
growing collection in an arena not waste every earlier size it passed through.
Accepting rather than refusing is deliberate: it lets an arena stand in for any allocator in generic code
that releases what it takes.

params.markdown: the layout it was allocated with

doc.returns: nothing when the release was accepted, or why it was refused

doc.summary: Grows or shrinks a block, extending the most recent allocation in place where it can.
doc.markdown:
Grows or shrinks a block, extending the most recent allocation in place where it can.
The two layouts must share an alignment. Growing the most recent allocation extends it without moving when
the current block has room; anything else takes new storage and copies, leaving the old space behind for the
next reset to reclaim.
Shrinking to a zero-sized layout releases the block and reports the shared empty address rather than the one
it rewound off of, so the result is releasable with the layout it was asked for.

params.name: newLayout
params.markdown: the layout wanted, which must have the same alignment

doc.returns: the address the block is at afterwards, or why it was not resized

doc.summary: One heap-allocated value of `T`, owned by exactly one holder.
doc.markdown:
One heap-allocated value of `T`, owned by exactly one holder.
Move-only: its copy operation is prohibited and `~Box` releases its allocation. Transfer one with `<-`; the
source is then moved-out and reading it is rejected while compiling rather than at run time.
The storage is released when the box is destroyed, at whichever scope exit, return, `break`, `continue` or
overwriting assignment the value's life ends at.

doc.markdown:
Puts `value` on the heap and hands back the box that owns it.
`allocator` is borrowed for the call and kept in the box. `value` is consumed: on success the box owns it,
and on failure it is destroyed rather than leaked.
Runs in whatever time the allocator takes, and allocates exactly one block.

doc.summary: The value this box holds.
doc.markdown:
The value this box holds.
`self` is borrowed and stays the caller's; the pointer borrows the box's storage and is valid only while the
box is. Returns null for a box whose value has been taken out.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.
The pointer dies with the box. Holding it past a move of the box is holding a pointer into released storage.
doc.returns: the address of the held value, or null when the box is empty

doc.summary: Whether this box still holds a value.
doc.markdown:
Whether this box still holds a value.
`self` is borrowed. False only for a box whose value `TryTake` has moved out, which is a box that owns
nothing and releases nothing.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: whether the box holds nothing

doc.summary: Moves the value out of the box, leaving the box empty, and releases the storage.
doc.markdown:
Moves the value out of the box, leaving the box empty, and releases the storage.
`self` is borrowed mutably and is left empty. `destination` receives the value and must not be null; it is
left unwritten when this reports `false`, which happens only for a box that is already empty.
The storage goes back to the allocator here rather than at the box's destruction, so a caller taking the
value out does not have to keep the box alive afterwards.
Runs in whatever time the allocator takes.
doc.returns: whether there was a value to take

doc.summary: Destroys the value and releases its storage, if the box still holds any.
doc.markdown:
Destroys the value and releases its storage, if the box still holds any.
Runs when the box's life ends, and does nothing for a box whose value was taken out. A box that was moved
away is not destroyed where it used to live, so the storage is released exactly once.

doc.summary: The operations every allocator provides.
doc.markdown:
The operations every allocator provides.
Written as an interface so a generic can require it — `func Build<A: Allocator>(allocator: &var A)` borrows the
caller's allocator and resolves calls at each instantiation with nothing dispatched at run time.
No operation writes through its receiver: an implementation keeps its state behind a pointer, as the handles do,
so a copied allocator value draws from the same storage and a read-only view may allocate.

doc.summary: Takes storage matching `layout` and reports where it landed.
doc.markdown:
Takes storage matching `layout` and reports where it landed.
The address satisfies the layout's alignment. The contents are undefined.
A zero-sized layout gives a non-null aligned address that nothing may be read from or written to.
The storage is the caller's until `Deallocate` takes it back with an equal layout.
doc.returns: the address of the storage, or why none was taken

doc.summary: Gives back storage that this allocator handed out.
doc.markdown:
Gives back storage that this allocator handed out.
`block` must be an address this allocator returned, and `layout` must equal the layout it was given with.
Reports `InvalidBlock` where the allocator can tell, and is undefined where it cannot.
Every pointer into the block becomes invalid, and the storage may be handed to the next allocation at once.

params.markdown: the layout it was allocated with

doc.returns: nothing when the release was accepted, or why it was refused

doc.summary: Changes the size of a block, preserving as much of its contents as both layouts hold.
doc.markdown:
Changes the size of a block, preserving as much of its contents as both layouts hold.
`block` and `oldLayout` describe the existing allocation; `newLayout` is what is wanted. The address reported
may or may not be the address it was given, so the caller must use what comes back.
On success the first `min(old, new)` bytes are preserved and the original block is gone. On failure the
original block is untouched and still the caller's.
A `newLayout` of size zero reports the shared empty address, exactly as `Allocate` would, so the result is
always releasable with the layout it was asked for.
The two layouts must have the same alignment. An allocator reports `Unsupported` rather than silently moving
a block to a different alignment.
The old pointer is invalid once this succeeds, whether or not the address changed.

params.name: newLayout
params.markdown: the layout wanted, which must have the same alignment

doc.returns: the address the block is at afterwards, or why it was not resized

doc.summary: The address a zero-sized allocation reports.
doc.markdown:
The address a zero-sized allocation reports.
Not null, so a caller need not branch, and aligned to anything, so it satisfies every layout. Nothing may be read
from or written to it: it is an address that exists rather than storage that does.
Every allocator in this package returns exactly this for a zero-sized layout, which makes a zero-sized block
recognizable and its release free.

doc.summary: The address a zero-sized allocation reports, as a pointer.
doc.markdown:
The address a zero-sized allocation reports, as a pointer.
Takes nothing and returns the same value every time.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: the address every zero-sized allocation reports

doc.summary: Whether `block` is the address a zero-sized allocation reports.
doc.markdown:
Whether `block` is the address a zero-sized allocation reports.
`block` is read by value and never dereferenced.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.

params.name: block
params.markdown: the address to test, never dereferenced

doc.returns: whether it is the address a zero-sized allocation reports

doc.summary: Why an allocation, reallocation or release did not do what was asked.
doc.markdown: Why an allocation, reallocation or release did not do what was asked.

cases.name: Unsupported
cases.doc:
The layout cannot be served by this allocator at all: an alignment stricter than it can give, or a size it
could never hold. A different allocator might succeed; retrying with this one will not.

cases.name: OutOfMemory
cases.doc: The allocator has no storage left. A smaller request might succeed, and so might this one later.

cases.name: InvalidBlock
cases.doc:
The arguments do not describe an allocation this allocator handed out — a pointer it did not give, or a
layout that does not match the one it was given with. This is a caller's mistake rather than a shortage.

doc.summary: Whether a later attempt could plausibly succeed.
doc.markdown:
Whether a later attempt could plausibly succeed.
`self` is borrowed. True only for `OutOfMemory`, which is a shortage rather than a mistake: `Unsupported` and
`InvalidBlock` describe the request rather than the moment, so repeating either gives the same answer.
doc.returns: whether asking again later could succeed

doc.markdown:

Owns no storage and has no destructor, but prohibits copying because duplicated bump state could hand the same
bytes to two callers. Use `Handle` when a storable `Allocator` adapter is needed.

allocator rather than an error, and is what a caller testing exhaustion wants.

doc.summary: A validated allocation request: a size, and the alignment its address must satisfy.
doc.markdown:
A validated allocation request: a size, and the alignment its address must satisfy.
Copy and owns nothing. Every instance is valid, because `New` refuses to build an invalid one: the alignment is a
power of two, and the size rounded up to that alignment does not pass the end of the address space.
A size of zero is valid and is not an allocation of nothing — see `Allocate` for what an allocator does with it.

doc.markdown:
A layout for one value of `T`, using its actual size and alignment.
No value is copied or consumed. Cannot fail, runs in constant time, and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: `T`'s own size and alignment

doc.summary: A layout for `count` consecutive values of `T`, or absent when the size would overflow.
doc.markdown:
A layout for `count` consecutive values of `T`, or absent when the size would overflow.
No value is copied or consumed. A zero count describes empty storage at `T`'s alignment.
Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: the array layout, or `none` if its size cannot be represented

members.name: New
members.signature: pub func New(size: uint, alignment: uint) -> Layout?

doc.summary: A layout for `size` bytes at `alignment`, or nothing when the pair cannot be one.
doc.markdown:
A layout for `size` bytes at `alignment`, or nothing when the pair cannot be one.
`size` and `alignment` are read by value; the layout is returned by copy. Reports `none` when `alignment` is
zero or not a power of two, and when rounding `size` up to `alignment` would pass the end of the address
space — which is the case that turns into an allocation far smaller than the caller asked for if it is not
caught here.
Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.

params.name: alignment
params.markdown: the boundary the address must be a multiple of

doc.returns: the layout, or `none` when `alignment` is not a usable power of two

doc.summary: A layout for `size` bytes at the alignment a machine word wants.
doc.markdown:
A layout for `size` bytes at the alignment a machine word wants.
`size` is read by value. Reports `none` only when rounding `size` up would pass the end of the address space,
since the alignment is known good.
This is the layout for storage whose contents are bytes rather than a typed value: an allocation aligned to a
word suits anything the machine loads in one instruction.
Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: a layout of that size at its natural alignment, or `none` when there is none

doc.summary: The size this layout occupies once rounded up to its own alignment.
doc.markdown:
The size this layout occupies once rounded up to its own alignment.
`self` is borrowed. This is the stride between two of these laid out one after another, and is what an arena
advances by. Cannot overflow, because `New` refused every size for which it would.
Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: the size rounded up to a whole number of alignments

members.name: IsSatisfiedBy
members.signature: pub func IsSatisfiedBy(self: &Layout, address: uint) -> bool

doc.summary: Whether `address` satisfies this layout's alignment.
doc.markdown:
Whether `address` satisfies this layout's alignment.
`self` is borrowed and `address` is read by value and never dereferenced.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: whether `address` meets this layout's alignment

doc.summary: Whether two layouts ask for the same thing.
doc.markdown:
Whether two layouts ask for the same thing.
`self` is borrowed and `other` is read by value.
doc.returns: whether both the size and the alignment match

doc.summary: Whether two layouts ask for different things.
doc.markdown: Whether two layouts ask for different things.
doc.returns: whether either the size or the alignment differs

doc.summary: The alignment a value of `size` bytes naturally wants.
doc.markdown:
The alignment a value of `size` bytes naturally wants.
`size` is read by value. Returns the largest power of two that divides a value of this size, capped at a machine
word, which is what every supported target's ABI requires of an ordinary value.
A size of zero reports one, since a zero-sized value has nothing to align.
Runs in time proportional to the word size and allocates nothing.

params.name: size
params.markdown: the size to choose an alignment for

doc.returns: the largest useful power-of-two alignment for that size

doc.summary: How many size classes a pool serves.
doc.markdown: How many size classes a pool serves.

doc.summary: The smallest size class, and so the block a one-byte request occupies.
doc.markdown:
The smallest size class, and so the block a one-byte request occupies.
Large enough to hold the link a free block stores in its own storage, which is what lets a free list cost nothing
beyond the blocks already on it.

doc.summary: The largest size class.
doc.markdown: The largest size class. A request past this goes to the backing allocator instead.

doc.summary: The alignment every chunk is taken at, and so the strictest alignment a pooled block can satisfy.
doc.markdown:
The alignment every chunk is taken at, and so the strictest alignment a pooled block can satisfy.
Every class is a multiple of this, so every block carved from a chunk is aligned to it as well.

doc.summary: How many blocks a chunk holds when the caller does not say.
doc.markdown: How many blocks a chunk holds when the caller does not say.

doc.summary: One chunk of pool storage, carved into blocks of a single class.
doc.markdown:
One chunk of pool storage, carved into blocks of a single class.
Never constructed by a caller. The blocks follow the header, and the header records what the chunk was taken with
so that releasing or re-carving it needs nothing else.

fields.name: previous
fields.doc: The chunk taken before this one, or null for the first.

fields.name: total
fields.doc: The total size the chunk was taken with, header included.

fields.name: classIndex
fields.doc: Which class this chunk was carved into.

fields.name: blocks
fields.doc: How many blocks it was carved into.

doc.summary: An allocator that serves small blocks from per-class free lists.
doc.markdown:
An allocator that serves small blocks from per-class free lists.
Move-only, because it owns its chunks. Pass it to something expecting an `Allocator` through `Handle`, which
borrows rather than moves.

fields.name: backing
fields.doc: Where the chunks come from.

fields.name: free
fields.doc:
The first free block of each class, by address, or zero for a class with none.
Held as addresses rather than pointers because a free block's link lives in the block's own storage, which is
not a value of any type until the block is handed out again.

fields.name: chunks
fields.doc: The most recently taken chunk, or null before the first request.

fields.name: blocksPerChunk
fields.doc: How many blocks each new chunk is carved into.

fields.name: live
fields.doc: How many pooled blocks are currently handed out.

fields.name: chunkCount
fields.doc: How many chunks the pool holds.

members.name: Pool
members.signature: pub func Pool(backing: Allocator, blocksPerChunk: uint) -> Pool

doc.summary: A pool that will take its chunks from `backing`.
doc.markdown:
A pool that will take its chunks from `backing`.
`backing` is borrowed for the call and kept. `blocksPerChunk` is how many blocks each chunk is carved into;
zero asks for the default. Cannot fail and allocates nothing: the first chunk is taken when the first request
arrives, so a pool that is never used costs nothing.

params.name: backing
params.markdown: where the pool's chunks come from

params.name: blocksPerChunk
params.markdown: how many blocks a chunk carves into; zero asks for the default

doc.returns: the pool, holding no chunk yet

doc.summary: A copyable interface adapter pointing at this pool.
doc.markdown:
A copyable interface adapter pointing at this pool.
`self` stays the caller's. Allocations through the handle update this pool rather than copied state.
Cannot fail. Runs in constant time and allocates nothing.
The handle borrows the pool and must not outlive it, nor survive the pool being moved.
doc.returns: a copyable adapter pointing at this pool

doc.summary: Takes every pooled block back at once, keeping the chunks for the next round of work.
doc.markdown:
Takes every pooled block back at once, keeping the chunks for the next round of work.
`self` is borrowed mutably. Every pooled pointer the pool handed out becomes invalid, including any a caller
still holds. The chunks are kept and carved again, so a second round of the same work asks the backing
allocator for nothing.
Blocks that went to the backing allocator because they were too large or too strictly aligned are not
touched, and are still the caller's to release.
Runs in time proportional to the number of blocks. Cannot fail.
Nothing may be read from or written to any pooled allocation afterwards.

doc.summary: How many pooled blocks are currently handed out.
doc.markdown:
How many pooled blocks are currently handed out.
`self` is borrowed. Blocks that went to the backing allocator are not counted, because the pool does not
track them.
doc.returns: how many blocks are currently handed out

doc.summary: How many chunks the pool has taken from its backing allocator.
doc.markdown:
How many chunks the pool has taken from its backing allocator.
`self` is borrowed. Zero before the first request.
doc.returns: how many chunks the pool holds

members.name: ClassSize
members.signature: pub func ClassSize(self: &Pool, index: uint) -> uint

doc.summary: The block size of class `index`, or zero for an index past the last class.
doc.markdown:
The block size of class `index`, or zero for an index past the last class.
`self` is borrowed. Classes run from `PoolSmallestClass` to `PoolLargestClass`, doubling.
doc.returns: the block size that class serves

doc.summary: Gives every chunk back to the backing allocator.
doc.markdown:
Gives every chunk back to the backing allocator.
Runs when the pool's life ends. Every pooled pointer the pool handed out becomes invalid. Blocks that went to
the backing allocator directly are not released here and are still the caller's.

doc.summary: A copyable interface adapter pointing at a pool.
doc.markdown:
A copyable interface adapter pointing at a pool.
A handle is cheap to copy and may be stored wherever an allocator is wanted, but it does not own the pool.

fields.name: pool
fields.doc: The pool this borrows. Never null for a handle `Pool::Handle` produced.

members.name: Allocate
members.signature: pub func Allocate(self: &PoolHandle, layout: Layout) -> (*var opaque) ! AllocError

doc.summary: Takes a block of the smallest class that holds `layout`.
doc.markdown:
Takes a block of the smallest class that holds `layout`.
`result` receives the address when this reports `None`. A zero-sized layout gives the shared empty block. A
layout too large for the largest class, or needing an alignment stricter than `PoolAlignment`, is passed to
the backing allocator unchanged.
Takes a chunk when the class has no free block, which is the only path here that can fail. Otherwise runs in
constant time.
The block lives until it is released, the pool is reset, or the pool is destroyed.
doc.returns: the address of the storage, or why none was taken

members.name: Deallocate
members.signature: pub func Deallocate(self: &PoolHandle, block: *var opaque, layout: Layout) -> ! AllocError

doc.summary: Puts a block back on the free list of the class its layout names.
doc.markdown:
Puts a block back on the free list of the class its layout names.
`layout` must equal the one the block was taken with, which is what tells the pool whether the block is its
own or the backing allocator's. A block that went to the backing allocator is released there.
Runs in constant time, and cannot fail for a pooled block.
The block may be handed to the next allocation of its class at once.

params.name: layout
params.markdown: the layout it was allocated with

doc.returns: nothing when the release was accepted, or why it was refused

members.name: Reallocate
members.signature: pub func Reallocate(self: &PoolHandle, block: *var opaque, oldLayout: Layout, newLayout: Layout) -> (*var opaque) ! AllocError

doc.summary: Changes the size of a block, which costs nothing when both sizes land in the same class.
doc.markdown:
Changes the size of a block, which costs nothing when both sizes land in the same class.
The two layouts must share an alignment. A block whose new size fits the class it already occupies comes back
unmoved — growing a 20-byte allocation to 30 does not touch storage at all. Anything else takes a new block,
copies, and releases the old one.

params.name: newLayout
params.markdown: the layout wanted, which must have the same alignment

doc.returns: the address the block is at afterwards, or why it was not resized

doc.summary: The class a layout belongs to, or `PoolClassCount` for a layout no class can serve.
doc.markdown:
The class a layout belongs to, or `PoolClassCount` for a layout no class can serve.
`layout` is read by value. A size past `PoolLargestClass`, or an alignment stricter than `PoolAlignment`, has no
class, and the caller passes it to the backing allocator instead.
The answer depends only on the layout, which is what lets a release reach the same conclusion as the allocation
it matches without the pool recording anything per block.
Cannot fail. Runs in time proportional to the number of classes and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: the index of the class that serves it, or the class count when none does

doc.summary: What a system allocation records about itself, immediately before the address the caller sees.
doc.markdown:
What a system allocation records about itself, immediately before the address the caller sees.
Never constructed by a caller. The magic is checked on release, which is what turns a mismatched or foreign
pointer into a reported `InvalidBlock` rather than a corrupted heap.

fields.name: magic
fields.doc: A fixed pattern, checked on release.

fields.name: base
fields.doc: The address the page layer gave, which is what has to be released.

fields.name: length
fields.doc: The length the page layer was given, which is what it has to be released with.

fields.name: size
fields.doc: The size the caller asked for, checked against the layout on release.

doc.summary: The pattern a valid system block header carries.
doc.markdown:
The pattern a valid system block header carries.
Chosen to be unlikely in ordinary data, so a pointer that was never one of these is very unlikely to look like
one. This is a check against a mistake, not against an adversary.

doc.summary: An allocator that asks the operating system for pages.
doc.markdown:
An allocator that asks the operating system for pages.
Carries no state: every instance behaves identically, and one may be created wherever it is needed rather than
passed around. It is `Copy` for that reason.
Page-granular, so a small allocation costs a whole page. Use it as the backing store for an arena or a pool
rather than for many small values directly.

fields.name: reserved
fields.doc: Present so the type is not empty; carries nothing and is never read.

doc.summary: Constructs a stateless system allocator.
doc.markdown:
Constructs a stateless system allocator.
The result is structural and copyable. Borrow it as `&var Allocator` when a temporary interface view is
sufficient; no adapter or owning conversion is required.
doc.returns: the allocator, which holds no state of its own

members.name: Allocate
members.signature: pub func Allocate(self: &SystemAllocator, layout: Layout) -> (*var opaque) ! AllocError

doc.summary: Takes storage matching `layout` from the operating system.
doc.markdown:
Takes storage matching `layout` from the operating system.
`result` receives the address when this reports `None`. A zero-sized layout gives the shared empty block and
takes nothing from the system.
Reports `Unsupported` for an alignment larger than the total the request would occupy, `OutOfMemory` when the
system refuses.
The storage is the caller's until `Deallocate` takes it back with an equal layout.
doc.returns: the address of the storage, or why none was taken

members.name: Deallocate
members.signature: pub func Deallocate(self: &SystemAllocator, block: *var opaque, layout: Layout) -> ! AllocError

doc.summary: Gives the storage behind `block` back to the operating system.
doc.markdown:
Gives the storage behind `block` back to the operating system.
`layout` must equal the one the block was allocated with. Reports `InvalidBlock` when the header is not
there or does not agree with the layout, which catches a foreign pointer and a mismatched size before either
reaches the page layer.
Every pointer into the block becomes invalid.

params.name: layout
params.markdown: the layout it was allocated with

doc.returns: nothing when the release was accepted, or why it was refused

members.name: Reallocate
members.signature: pub func Reallocate(self: &SystemAllocator, block: *var opaque, oldLayout: Layout, newLayout: Layout) -> (*var opaque) ! AllocError

doc.summary: Changes the size of a block by taking a new one and copying what fits.
doc.markdown:
Changes the size of a block by taking a new one and copying what fits.
The two layouts must share an alignment; anything else reports `Unsupported` rather than moving the block to
a different one. On success the original block is released and `result` holds the new address, which is
generally not the old one.
This allocator never grows a block in place, even when the page it sits in has room: doing so would need a
free-list it deliberately does not keep.
The old pointer is invalid once this succeeds. On failure it is untouched and still the caller's.

params.name: newLayout
params.markdown: the layout wanted, which must have the same alignment

doc.returns: the address the block is at afterwards, or why it was not resized
